lesson.title: Mixing Orbitals to Match a Molecule's Shape
lesson.summary: Hybridization is the model chemists use to reshape an atom's ordinary atomic orbitals into a new set of equivalent orbitals that point exactly where VSEPR says the bonds and lone pairs need to go.
lesson.body:
Atomic orbitals, on their own, do a poor job of explaining the molecules chemists actually observe. Take carbon: its ground state electron configuration is 1s2 2s2 2p2, which gives it only two unpaired electrons in separate 2p orbitals. That configuration suggests carbon should form two bonds at roughly 90 degrees, the angle between p orbitals. Yet methane, CH4, has four completely identical C-H bonds arranged at 109.5 degrees. Pure, unmodified atomic orbitals cannot account for either the number of bonds or the angle between them, and this gap between simple orbital theory and observed geometry is exactly the problem hybridization was built to solve.

Linus Pauling's solution was to treat the atomic orbitals on a single atom as mathematically mixable. Rather than keeping the 2s orbital and the three 2p orbitals as separate, differently shaped regions, you combine them into a new set of hybrid orbitals that are all equivalent to each other and point in the directions that minimize electron repulsion, which is to say, the directions VSEPR already predicts. The number of hybrid orbitals produced always equals the number of atomic orbitals mixed, which in turn always equals the number of electron domains around that atom: every bond and every lone pair needs its own hybrid orbital to sit in.

For carbon in methane, one 2s orbital mixes with all three 2p orbitals to produce four new sp3 hybrid orbitals. Each one is identical, with 25 percent s character and 75 percent p character, and the four of them point toward the corners of a tetrahedron, spaced 109.5 degrees apart. This single picture accounts for both observations that pure atomic orbitals could not: four equivalent bonds, at the correct angle. Every C-H sigma bond in methane forms from the head on overlap of one of these sp3 hybrids with a hydrogen 1s orbital.

The number of electron domains around an atom sets which hybridization it adopts, and this gives a direct bridge from counting domains, which you already do for VSEPR, to naming a hybridization. Two domains call for sp hybridization and a linear arrangement. Three domains call for sp2 hybridization and a trigonal planar arrangement. Four domains call for sp3 hybridization and a tetrahedral arrangement. The next few concepts work through each of these cases individually, using real molecules to show how the same counting rule that predicts molecular geometry also predicts which atomic orbitals mix.

It is worth being precise about what hybridization is and is not. It is a model for the orbitals on one particular atom, describing how that atom's own valence orbitals reorganize to build bonds; only valence orbitals hybridize, while inner, core electrons are left alone. It is not a replacement for VSEPR, but a companion to it: VSEPR tells you the shape a molecule adopts to minimize repulsion, and hybridization gives you the physical orbital picture of how the central atom's bonds achieve that shape. Keeping this relationship straight, VSEPR for shape, hybridization for orbitals, makes the rest of bonding theory far easier to follow.
